expert_opinion.location: Discussion - Summary of Findings and Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood (lines 781-815); Results - Demographic Controls (lines 590-618, Table 4); References (lines 1121-1125)
expert_opinion.quote:
Additionally, women rated Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more

important indicators of adulthood, and they reported higher achievement of Normative

Compliance. This result supports prior findings of higher ratings of importance for Normative

Compliance items for women among both American and Chinese participants, though no other

sex differences were reported (Badger et al., 2006). Other research also documented women

rating Normative Compliance as more important than men did, though they also found women

rated other constructs as important for this transition (Nelson et al., 2007). The lack of difference

in achievement in our sample is a curious finding that should be further considered, but the

pattern of perceived importance seems consistent with prior literature.

Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood

       Although replication of these age and gender effects are important, it was the replication

of associations with institutional selectivity and liberal arts status that represented our primary

questions. Specifically, we replicated Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) who first examined these

variables.
expert_opinion.reason: Using independent multi-site survey data from EAMMi2 (N = 1,572 students across 23 institutions), the authors empirically tested age and gender fixed effects across all four Markers of Adulthood importance and achievement subscales in Results ('Demographic Controls', lines 590-618, Table 4) and explicitly state in the Discussion that they 'replicated previously observed age and gender differences in markers of adulthood (Badger et al., 2006, Nelson et al., 2007)' (lines 781-782) and refer to the 'replication of these age and gender effects' (line 809). They directly compare their gender results (women rating Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more important and reporting higher Normative Compliance achievement) to Badger, S., Nelson, L. J., & Barry, C. M. (2006), 'Perceptions of the transition to adulthood among Chinese and American emerging adults', International Journal of Behavioral Development, 30(1), 84-93, doi:10.1177/0165025406062128, which reported higher female importance ratings for Normative Compliance among Chinese and American emerging adults with no other sex differences. Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) is not an intermediary replication chain for these effects because it treated biological sex and age only as covariates when testing institutional selectivity and liberal arts status (lines 186-190, 809-817). The only shipped row (input_row_index 2425, originally citing the psychometric manuscript Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman, 2016, and source-adjudicated to target_index 0, Fosse & Toyokawa, 2016) and sibling target_index 2 (Nelson et al., 2007, a separate Journal of Family Psychology study of emerging adults and their parents) are distinct works, so report equivalence does not apply. Note: prior_state_path was absent in the frozen snapshot and prior_adjudication_path adjudicated only input_row_index 2425 (target_index 0).

source_evidence.role: explicit demographic replication attribution
source_evidence.quote:
We replicated previously observed age and gender differences in markers of adulthood

(Badger et al., 2006, Nelson et al., 2007). First, age was associated with achievement for three of

four scales, but not with importance. This finding reflects a basic premise of EA. With increased
 age, individuals transition across these various MoAs (Arnett, 2000), but even the youngest

emerging adults may still rate these markers as important to achieve in the future. These findings

provide an important validity check of the scale generally.

source_evidence.quote:
In addition to demonstrating small inter-institutional differences, Fosse and Toyokawa

(2016) found, after controlling for respondents’ biological sex and age, individuals at more

selective institutions and liberal arts institutions reported less perceived importance and reduced
 likelihood of achieving Norm Compliance and Relational Maturity. Furthermore, individuals at

more selective institutions also reported lower attainment of Norm Compliance but slightly

higher attainment of Relational Maturity. These findings regarding institutional variability across

many EA dimensions for individuals at selective and liberal arts institutions should receive

further replication.

source_evidence.role: measured importance and achievement; same Fosse scoring
source_evidence.quote:
Markers of Adulthood (MoA). We measured 20 items associated with becoming an

adult derived from Arnett (1997; 2000). Respondents reported both how important the items are

to achieving adulthood on a 4 point scale (1, not at all; 4, very important) and the degree to

which they had achieved that marker on a 3 point scale (1, not at all; 2, somewhat; 3, yes) for the

four constructs identified by Fosse and Toyokawa (2016): Role Transition, Normative

Compliance, Relational Maturity, and Independence. For the scoring of achievement, we coded

“achievement” as 1 and “not achieved” as 0. Partial achievement (“somewhat”) was coded as

“not achieved”, consistent with Fosse and Toyokawa.

with Normative Compliance. In particular, men reported Normative Compliance as less

source_evidence.role: Results age and gender achievement comparisons
source_evidence.quote:
Achievement. Demographic variables significantly predicted achievement of all four

subscales. In particular, age was positively associated with achieving Role Transitions (b = .02),

Independence (b = .02), and Relational Maturity (b = .02), but not Normative Compliance. These

are unstandardized coefficients, and therefore, for each year of age, we predict .02 increase in

original units for these variables. Men reported lower levels of Normative Compliance

achievement (b = - .06) than women, but there was no evidence of other gender differences.

(this issue) examine the psychometric properties of these items, and because our question is

confirmatory rather than exploratory, we employed the constructs used by Fosse and Toyokawa

(2016). However, the explicit items included in each dimension are described in the Materials

actual_body_limits: The complete saved current manuscript, including all Methods, Results, Discussion, references and Table 4, is available and was inspected; it is not an original-body recovery for the cited 2006/2007/2016 reports.

No separate primary bodies for Badger 2006, Nelson 2007, Fosse/Toyokawa 2016 or Fosse/Grahe/Reifman 2016 were located in the bounded local original/new-text directories. Original-specific findings are therefore established through the current authors’ explicit accounts. No network acquisition was allowed or attempted.

The current paper establishes a 2004 EAMMI versus 2016 EAMMi2 distinction for its Fosse follow-up. It does not establish whether Badger 2006 and Nelson 2007 share any respondents, or give original-specific sample counts for them. Independent published findings do not require independent cohorts; neither cohort overlap nor report equivalence is decided from authors/year/DOI alone.

The Discussion states higher female Normative Compliance achievement and later says “The lack of difference in achievement in our sample”. Both statements are preserved. Results and Table 4 supply the actual contrasts; this context check assigns no outcome and does not resolve that prose tension.

many EA dimensions for individuals at selective and liberal arts institutions should receive

further replication.

source_evidence.role: measured importance and achievement; same Fosse scoring
source_evidence.quote:
Markers of Adulthood (MoA). We measured 20 items associated with becoming an

adult derived from Arnett (1997; 2000). Respondents reported both how important the items are

to achieving adulthood on a 4 point scale (1, not at all; 4, very important) and the degree to

which they had achieved that marker on a 3 point scale (1, not at all; 2, somewhat; 3, yes) for the

four constructs identified by Fosse and Toyokawa (2016): Role Transition, Normative

Compliance, Relational Maturity, and Independence. For the scoring of achievement, we coded

“achievement” as 1 and “not achieved” as 0. Partial achievement (“somewhat”) was coded as

“not achieved”, consistent with Fosse and Toyokawa.

prior_objections_and_report_chain.prior_duplicate_objection: Original three-target Luna packet incorrectly treated target 0 as a possible extra pair by comparing only the obsolete shipped psychometric identity. Parent pairing reconciliation /records/6 and candidate index /105 supersede it; successor /485 assigns only targets 1 and 2. Row 2425 is already corrected and parent-approved for Fosse/Toyokawa’s institutional finding. Do not export target 0 again.
prior_objections_and_report_chain.closest_chain: The current paper directly assigns the earlier demographic comparisons to Badger and Nelson; its Fosse overview and institutional Discussion instead identify institutional selectivity/liberal-arts findings from 2004 EAMMI. These positive finding-specific accounts support the two demographic targets beyond row 2425. Fosse’s use of age/sex controls is not by itself a rule excluding empirical findings or an intermediary relationship; the uninspected Fosse body cannot be declared to contain none.
prior_objections_and_report_chain.sibling_report_comparison: Badger is described as Chinese/American emerging adults with the female Normative Compliance importance finding and no other sex differences. Nelson is separately described as women rating Normative Compliance and other constructs as important, and its reference identifies emerging-adult/parent criteria. These are separate attributed published comparisons in the current source, not a presumption of disjoint cohorts. The current does not label Nelson as a later report of Badger’s same finding or Fosse as their closest demographic replication.
prior_objections_and_report_chain.method_only_objection: All three earlier references also contribute to dimension/scoring construction. That role does not erase the actual demographic estimates in Results/Table 4 and the explicit Discussion comparisons. Secondary validity checks and control variables can empirically retest a published finding.

actual_body_limits: The complete saved current manuscript, including all Methods, Results, Discussion, references and Table 4, is available and was inspected; it is not an original-body recovery for the cited 2006/2007/2016 reports.

No separate primary bodies for Badger 2006, Nelson 2007, Fosse/Toyokawa 2016 or Fosse/Grahe/Reifman 2016 were located in the bounded local original/new-text directories. Original-specific findings are therefore established through the current authors’ explicit accounts. No network acquisition was allowed or attempted.

The current paper establishes a 2004 EAMMI versus 2016 EAMMi2 distinction for its Fosse follow-up. It does not establish whether Badger 2006 and Nelson 2007 share any respondents, or give original-specific sample counts for them. Independent published findings do not require independent cohorts; neither cohort overlap nor report equivalence is decided from authors/year/DOI alone.

The Discussion states higher female Normative Compliance achievement and later says “The lack of difference in achievement in our sample”. Both statements are preserved. Results and Table 4 supply the actual contrasts; this context check assigns no outcome and does not resolve that prose tension.
